intro: Our research programs span discovery immunology to preclinical translation, with a strong focus on clinically grounded questions.

themes.title: Immune tolerance and autoimmunity
themes.text:
The immune system must perform a delicate balancing act. It must respond rapidly to infection and cancer while avoiding harmful responses against self. Our lab studies how this balance is established, maintained, and broken by focusing on the antigens recognized by T cells in autoimmune and inflammatory disease. We are especially interested in the earliest stages of immune education and in the tissue-specific antigenic cues that guide protective, tolerogenic, or pathogenic T cell responses across the life course.

We study antigen-specific T cell responses in settings including early-life tolerance, autoimmune arthritis, and immune-related adverse events that arise during cancer immunotherapy, as well as diseases in which infection may help trigger or amplify pathology through chronic antigen exposure or molecular mimicry. A major goal is to identify the self and non-self antigens seen by disease-associated T cells and to define the receptors and cellular states linked to those responses. By understanding exactly what T cells see in health and disease, we aim to reveal fundamental principles of immune tolerance and uncover new opportunities for therapies that restore immune balance with greater precision than broad immunosuppression.

themes.title: Ligand discovery and immune recognition
themes.text:
A central challenge in immunology is determining which ligands are recognized by T cells and how those recognition events shape cell function. Our lab develops and applies functional genomic, synthetic biology, and high-throughput screening approaches to discover the antigens, ligands, and antigen presentation pathways that underlie T cell recognition. We are particularly interested in questions that have been difficult to solve with conventional methods. What do disease-associated T cells actually recognize? Which host or pathogen-derived molecules trigger those responses? How are those targets generated, processed, and displayed in tissues? And how do different classes of T cells, including both αβ and γδ T cells, sample the molecular landscape of health and disease?

To answer these questions, we build scalable experimental systems that move from a T cell phenotype or receptor to the molecule it recognizes and to the cellular pathways that generate and present that target. Our work combines pooled CRISPR screens, TCR-MAP, synthetic biology, ribosome profiling, immunopeptidomics, and high-dimensional immune profiling to better define the antigens that are truly processed, presented, and recognized by T cells. We are also interested in developing new technologies that increase the scale and precision of T cell specificity mapping. These approaches allow us to study immune recognition across autoimmunity, infection, and cancer, including how infectious exposures such as EBV shape T cell responses and how microbial triggers may contribute to chronic inflammatory disease through persistent antigen exposure or molecular mimicry. By defining what T cells see, how those targets are displayed, and how recognition changes across disease contexts, we aim to uncover general principles of immune specificity that apply across many diseases.

themes.title: TCR discovery and engineering (αβ and γδ) for cancer translation
themes.text: We discover naturally primed αβ and γδ TCRs and engineer receptor formats for translational oncology programs. By combining specificity mapping, safety profiling, and functional testing, we prioritize candidates with strong anti-tumor potential and favorable developability for clinical-forward collaboration.
